name: Universal Orlando Mardi Gras
summary: The best-value thing Universal Orlando runs, because there is no ticket: a night parade, a concert series, and a street of Cajun food booths, all included with regular admission to Universal Studios Florida. The catch is that the good parts run on select nights and the concert brings the whole of Central Florida with it.
h1: Universal Orlando Mardi Gras: what is included, what the food costs, and which nights to pick
title: Universal Orlando Mardi Gras
description: Universal Orlando's Mardi Gras runs on regular admission at Universal Studios Florida. What is included, what the food costs, and which nights to plan around.

typicalWindow.endsAround: late March, and in recent seasons into April
typicalWindow.hours: Regular park hours across the whole window. The parade and the concerts run on selected evenings rather than nightly, and the per-night calendar Universal publishes is the only reliable guide to which.

pricing.cheapestNights: Weeknights early in the run, before the concert calendar fills out
pricing.priciestNights: Concert nights, and any Saturday in the second half of the run
notes: There is no Mardi Gras ticket. The parade, the concerts, and the street entertainment are included with regular admission to Universal Studios Florida, which makes this the cheapest event on the resort's calendar by a wide margin.
The range above is not an admission price. It is roughly what one item at the food booths has run, and that food is the only spend the event genuinely adds.
A tasting lanyard covering a fixed number of items has been sold each season. It pays for itself only if you commit to the full count, which two people sharing plates rarely reach.
Portions are tasting-sized rather than meal-sized. Two adults grazing the booths will spend more than a quick-service meal costs and eat rather less than one.
We do not publish a booth menu on this page. The lineup is rewritten between cycles and a carried-over menu with carried-over prices is the exact thing this site exists not to do.

whatYouGet: A night parade with floats and costumed riders throwing beads into the crowd, running on selected evenings and included with admission. The beads are free and there are a great many of them.

A concert series on selected nights, staged on the park's outdoor concert stage and included with admission rather than sold as an add-on. The lineup is announced in stages ahead of the season and is different every year.
The French Quarter Courtyard, a run of booths serving Cajun and Creole dishes in tasting portions, priced per item.
Street entertainment through the evening on parade nights: brass bands, stilt walkers, and performers working the route before the floats step off.
A seasonal Tribute Store build-out in the New York area, themed to the season and free to walk through.
The whole of Universal Studios Florida operating normally around it, because this is an overlay on an ordinary park day rather than a replacement for one.
whatYouDont: The parade every night. It runs on selected evenings, weighted toward weekends early in the run, and the calendar is published night by night. Turning up on the wrong Tuesday gets you the decoration and nothing else.

A quiet evening on a concert night. Those bring a local crowd that arrives for the band and stays for nothing else, and the walkways near the stage become impassable for about an hour on either side of the set.
Free food. The booths are the one part of this that costs money, and the portions are small enough that a couple working their way down the courtyard spends real money for a light dinner.
A lineup you can plan around months out. Concert acts are announced in stages, and the order of the announcements is not the order of the calendar.
Any ride benefit. Waits do not fall during the event, and on concert nights they rise, because the park is holding more people than an ordinary February evening.
An Islands of Adventure or Epic Universe component. This one sits entirely inside Universal Studios Florida, so a single-park ticket for the wrong park sees none of it.

verdict.short: Worth timing a day around if you are already visiting between February and April. Not worth building a trip around, and not worth booking blind on a concert lineup nobody has announced.
worthItIf: Your dates already fall inside the window and Universal Studios Florida was on the plan anyway. There is no ticket, so the event costs you nothing except the crowd it brings.
You will eat your way down the food booths. That is the part with the clearest value and the only part that costs anything.
You want a night parade at Universal Orlando, which the resort does not otherwise run.
You are traveling with teenagers who will not tolerate a daytime-only park plan, and you want an evening that justifies staying until close.
You are an annual passholder in Central Florida, in which case the marginal cost of an evening here is a parking fee.
skipIf: You are choosing travel dates purely for this. It is an overlay rather than a destination event, and February at Universal Orlando has better arguments for it than Mardi Gras.
Crowds bother you and your only options are concert nights. Those are the busiest evenings this park sees between the New Year and spring break.
You are traveling with small children and the parade is the plan. It runs late, the route is dense, and the beads come down over the heads of adults.
You need to know the concert lineup before you book. It will not all be public in time, and the acts announced first are not necessarily the ones on your dates.
Your ticket is single-park for Islands of Adventure or Epic Universe. None of this happens at either of them.

strategy.heading: Check the nightly calendar before you fix the day
body: The parade and the concerts run on selected evenings rather than every night, and that single fact decides whether your visit contains an event at all. Universal publishes the calendar night by night, and it is the only thing on this page worth checking before you book a park day.

The run starts thin and thickens. Early in the window the parade tends to be a weekend item; by the back half of the run it appears on more nights of the week. If your dates are in February, treat a parade night as the thing you plan around rather than something you hope to catch.
A night with the parade and no concert is the best combination on the calendar. You get the event content without the crowd that a headline act pulls in, and the food booths stay walkable.
If your only date has neither, the courtyard booths and the decoration still run through the whole window. That is a pleasant hour, not an evening, and it is worth setting expectations accordingly.

strategy.heading: Where to stand for the parade
body: Stand on the far stretch of the route rather than near the park entrance. The densest viewing forms where people stop walking, which is the first open stretch they reach after coming through the gates, and the back half of the route holds a fraction of the crowd for exactly the same parade.

Get into position about twenty minutes ahead on an ordinary parade night and about forty on a concert night. Longer than that is wasted; shorter than that on a busy night puts you three deep behind people with children on their shoulders.

Beads come down toward the front of the crowd, so the second row is a worse place to stand than either the first or the fifth. If catching beads matters to anyone in your group, commit to the curb or do not bother.
Leave before the last float rather than after it. The route empties into the same walkways in one movement, and five minutes of patience at the end costs twenty at the exit.

strategy.heading: Eating the French Quarter Courtyard properly
body: Eat before the parade, not after it. The booths take their heaviest run the moment the floats finish, and the queues at that point are longer than anything the event has otherwise produced.

Order across the group and share. Portions are tasting-sized by design, and four people ordering four different things and splitting them covers more of the menu for less money than four people each buying a meal-shaped plate.

Do the arithmetic on the tasting lanyard before you buy it. It is priced against a fixed number of items, and it only wins if your group genuinely eats that many. Sharing plates is usually what stops people reaching the count.

We are not publishing a menu here. The booth lineup and the prices are rewritten between cycles, and a menu carried over from last season is the kind of thing that reads as helpful and is actively wrong by the time anyone uses it.

strategy.heading: Concert nights, and the one hour they hand you
body: The concert is genuinely included, which is unusual enough to be worth saying twice: this is a full set from a touring act on a regular park ticket. If you like the act, it is the best-value hour Universal Orlando sells all year.

If you do not know the act, use the set as ride time. The concert hour is the one hour of a Mardi Gras evening when standby queues across the park drop noticeably, because a large share of the park is standing in one place watching a band.
Standing room fills from the front and it fills early. On a headline night the area in front of the stage has filled well before the set starts, and there is no reserved seating to fall back on.
Plan the exit rather than the arrival. Concert nights empty the park in a single movement at close, and the walk out through CityWalk is the slowest part of the evening.

faqs.q: Do I need a separate ticket for Mardi Gras?
faqs.a: No. The parade, the concerts, the street entertainment, and the decoration are all included with regular admission to Universal Studios Florida. The only thing that costs extra is the food at the booths. That makes this the cheapest event on Universal Orlando's calendar and the easiest one to add to a trip you were taking anyway.

faqs.q: Does the parade run every night?
faqs.a: No. It runs on selected evenings, weighted toward weekends early in the run and appearing on more nights as the season goes on. Universal publishes a night-by-night calendar, and that calendar is the thing to check before you commit a park day. A visit on a night without the parade gets you the courtyard booths and the decoration only.

faqs.q: Who is playing the concerts this year?
faqs.a: We do not publish a lineup we cannot source. Acts are announced in stages ahead of the season and the announcement order is not the calendar order, so any page listing a full lineup months out is either quoting last year or guessing. Check Universal's own event page for the dates you are considering, and treat the concert as a bonus rather than as the reason to book.

faqs.q: How much does the food cost?
faqs.a: Individual items have run roughly $7 to $16 each in recent seasons, in tasting portions rather than meal portions. A tasting lanyard covering a fixed number of items is also sold, and it only saves money if your group eats the full count. We do not list the booth menu here because it is rewritten between cycles and a stale menu is worse than none.

faqs.q: Is Mardi Gras suitable for children?
faqs.a: Yes, with one caveat. This is a regular park day with a night parade attached, and nothing about it is aimed at adults in the way Halloween Horror Nights is. The caveat is timing and density: the parade runs in the evening, the route gets packed, and the beads are thrown over the heads of standing adults. Younger children do better watching from the back half of the route.

faqs.q: Does any of this happen at Islands of Adventure or Epic Universe?
faqs.a: No. Mardi Gras sits entirely inside Universal Studios Florida. If you are holding a single-park ticket for either of the other two parks, you will see none of it, and a park-to-park ticket is the only version that lets you move between a daytime plan elsewhere and an evening here.

Early February through late March, and in recent seasons into April, on select nights within that window. As of July 2026 we have not verified an announcement of this cycle's dates, its parade calendar, or its concert lineup, so none of those are stated here. The window itself has been stable for years and is safe to plan around at the level of a month.
